frictionVectors.title: European Energy Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control through Sonatrach and pipeline/LNG exports, but European buyers are pressing for greater flexibility and pricing leverage. Hydrocarbon dependence leaves fiscal sovereignty exposed to global price swings.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya increases border-security costs and complicates Algeria's non-interventionist regional posture. External military and intelligence activity near its southern borders remains a sovereignty concern.

frictionVectors.title: External Oil Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Angola retains formal control over petroleum resources, but production, finance, and technology remain deeply tied to foreign operators and lenders. Declining output and debt-service pressures constrain sovereign bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting U.S., European, Chinese, and regional interest because of its route toward Congolese and Zambian critical minerals. Infrastructure investment could diversify Angola's leverage, but also create competing external dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Border Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger have been strained by sanctions-era political disputes and restrictions affecting trade through Benin's port system. The confrontation threatens customs revenue, regional connectivity, and Benin's role as a trusted transit hub.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Logistics Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's expansion strengthens Benin's economic sovereignty, but port modernization and logistics finance remain exposed to foreign capital and regional commercial interests. Dependence on Nigerian and Sahelian trade flows limits policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Partnership
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is using its market position to demand greater local value addition and a stronger share of diamond revenues. Negotiations with De Beers remain central to whether resource control translates into durable national development.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Diversification Race
frictionVectors.details: New interest in copper, nickel, lithium, and other minerals offers diversification but may introduce fresh foreign ownership and infrastructure dependencies. Botswana's regulatory credibility gives it comparatively strong leverage over investors.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Alignment
frictionVectors.details: The junta is reducing reliance on Western security partners and deepening ties with Russia, trading diplomatic flexibility for military support. The arrangement risks opaque concessions, sanctions exposure, and diminished oversight of strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-Sector Control
frictionVectors.details: Gold is the government's principal source of sovereign leverage, but insecurity, artisanal mining, smuggling, and foreign commercial interests weaken state capture of value. Efforts to nationalize or tighten control could raise revenue while deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Licensing
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked firms remain important in gold, nickel and rare-earth prospects, while weak oversight limits Burundi's ability to capture revenue and enforce local processing.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-DRC Border Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Regional conflict and diplomatic friction constrain border trade, security cooperation and access to eastern Congolese transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Port and Connectivity Assets
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport and digital infrastructure depend heavily on external finance and operators, creating long-term exposure over strategic Atlantic nodes.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries Access and Enforcement
frictionVectors.details: Limited surveillance capacity makes Cabo Verde reliant on foreign partnerships to protect its maritime resources and regulate distant-water fishing.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Financed Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external lenders remain central to major roads, energy and industrial projects, increasing debt-service and procurement leverage over national planning.

frictionVectors.title: Separatist and Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Anglophone regions and instability near Nigeria and the Central African Republic disrupt transport corridors, agricultural production and resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-Minerals Arrangements
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security actors and mining interests retain substantial influence, weakening transparency and limiting the state's independent control over gold and diamond revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-Group Control of Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Rebel and criminal networks continue to contest mining zones and trade routes, while neighboring states and external partners compete for security influence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Oil and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external firms remain deeply embedded in oil production, refining and export infrastructure, constraining domestic control of the energy chain.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Border and Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan war drives refugee flows, arms trafficking and cross-border militia risks, while competing foreign security relationships test N'Djamena's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France's administration of Mayotte remains the central sovereignty dispute, limiting Comoros' control over surrounding maritime space and associated fisheries and seabed resources.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on remittances, Gulf and international aid, and imported fuel, constraining its bargaining power over infrastructure and resource development.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and Copper Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in copper and cobalt production, while Kinshasa is pressing for stronger contract terms and greater domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Regional Intervention
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east, including alleged Rwandan support for M23, continues to undermine state control over territory, transport corridors, and mineral supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and Gulf investment strengthen Egypt's liquidity but increase outside influence over strategic assets, land, and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile allocation
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam remains Cairo's central sovereignty and water-security concern.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil output and opaque revenue management leave the state dependent on a narrow resource base and vulnerable to external energy partners.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore gas competition
frictionVectors.details: Regional competition and foreign technical capital shape the viability of Equatorial Guinea's LNG and downstream ambitions, limiting autonomous control over development.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector opacity
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects generate strategic revenue but rely on foreign operators and remain difficult to assess because of limited transparency and restricted oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping routes attract competing regional and external security interests, raising sovereignty risks around ports and maritime infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Economic reliance on South Africa
frictionVectors.details: Trade, customs arrangements, energy links, and remittances tie Eswatini's economic space closely to South Africa, reducing room for independent infrastructure strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and land-market exposure
frictionVectors.details: The sugar sector and related land interests remain vulnerable to changing trade preferences, external standards, and foreign commercial influence.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam increases Ethiopia's strategic control over electricity and water infrastructure while sustaining acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on Chinese, Gulf, and other external capital give partners leverage over major transport, energy, and industrial projects.

highlights: Oil and Manganese Assets Under Renegotiation

frictionVectors.title: French and Chinese Resource Competition
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is seeking more favorable terms from established French operators while expanding Chinese involvement in mining and infrastructure. The government’s sovereignty agenda is constrained by financing and technical dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Transgabon Railway and Export Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Rail and port reliability remains critical to manganese and timber exports. Infrastructure weaknesses limit state leverage over multinational producers and expose the economy to external logistics providers.

highlights: Fisheries and Energy Sovereignty Under Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Industrial Fishing
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked fleets and weak monitoring continue to threaten domestic fisheries and food security. Limited enforcement capacity reduces The Gambia’s ability to capture the full value of its maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on Senegalese Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Trade, fuel access, transport, and electricity remain closely tied to Senegalese corridors and regional arrangements. This dependence supports stability but narrows Banjul’s strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Mining and Environmental Degradation
frictionVectors.details: Unregulated gold mining damages farmland and water systems while involving domestic political networks and foreign-linked supply chains. Efforts to formalize the sector are strengthening state oversight but remain contested.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Investment Terms
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is seeking greater domestic processing and value retention in gold, bauxite, and emerging lithium projects. Fiscal pressure and reliance on external capital may limit its bargaining power with multinational investors.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou China-Rio Tinto Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore complex is generating major infrastructure investment but remains dominated by foreign consortia and export-oriented logistics. Conakry’s challenge is converting resource rents into durable domestic industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Corridor and Local Discontent
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite production depends heavily on foreign operators, dedicated railways, and port infrastructure. Land pressure, environmental damage, and opaque contract governance continue to fuel sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Cashew Trade
frictionVectors.details: Cashews provide the country’s main export income, yet traders, processors, and finance are largely external to the domestic economy. Limited processing capacity leaves producers vulnerable to price-setting and supply-chain shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, Narcotics, and Regional Influence
frictionVectors.details: Weak maritime and customs institutions create openings for illicit trafficking and foreign influence around port infrastructure. Dependence on regional security and commercial networks constrains Bissau’s effective sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Kenya balances IMF-linked fiscal reforms with major Chinese, Gulf, and Western financing interests. Debt-service pressures constrain its room to set infrastructure and energy priorities independently.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and the Northern Corridor remain strategically important, while competing regional routes and foreign-backed logistics projects test Kenya's control over trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water revenues and infrastructure are tied heavily to South African demand and financing. The arrangement provides critical income but limits bargaining power over pricing, maintenance, and long-term resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Power and fiscal vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic generation capacity and dependence on South African-linked systems expose Lesotho to supply disruptions and external policy decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and other mineral projects depend on foreign capital, concessions, and export infrastructure. Weak state capacity makes contract transparency and local value retention persistent sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Freeport and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and major transport corridors remain reliant on external operators and investors, giving foreign commercial actors substantial influence over trade and strategic infrastructure.

highlights: Foreign patrons shape security and exports

frictionVectors.title: Competing oil authorities
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to use control of oil fields, terminals, and the central banking system as leverage. Production remains vulnerable to blockades and factional bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: External military influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign states and private military networks retain influence through arms, advisers, and security partnerships. This weakens unified Libyan control over borders, energy infrastructure, and maritime access.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector foreign leverage
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, graphite, and ilmenite projects rely heavily on foreign investors and export markets. Madagascar faces continuing pressure to improve state revenue and domestic processing without deterring capital.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and transport bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable power and weak roads, ports, and logistics systems increase dependence on external project operators. These constraints limit the state's ability to capture more value from strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt distress and foreign-exchange shortages leave fiscal and import policy heavily influenced by the IMF and external creditors. Austerity risks constraining domestic policy space and public investment.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic minerals and energy access
frictionVectors.details: New uranium, rare-earth and graphite projects could broaden the export base, but licensing, infrastructure and foreign-investor dependence limit Malawi's leverage. Fuel and electricity shortages remain acute sovereignty constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-code confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are pressing foreign mining companies for larger state participation and revenue shares, particularly in gold. This strengthens formal resource control but risks arbitration, investment delays and production disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security realignment
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian security assistance has replaced much Western and regional cooperation, increasing military autonomy while creating strategic and financial dependence on Moscow. Persistent jihadist attacks continue to threaten mines, roads and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas project governance
frictionVectors.details: The Senegal-Mauritania Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers major fiscal and energy gains but requires sustained cross-border coordination and exposes Nouakchott to operator, pricing and downstream infrastructure leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and prospective green-hydrogen investments depend on foreign capital, port capacity and transport corridors. Chinese, Gulf and European partners compete for influence over logistics and future energy exports.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos settlement implementation
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago has advanced diplomatically, but implementation, base arrangements and regional security interests remain sensitive. The United Kingdom and United States retain substantial practical leverage around Diego Garcia.

frictionVectors.title: Blue-economy competition
frictionVectors.details: Indian Ocean shipping, fisheries and seabed resources attract interest from India, China, Europe and Gulf states. Mauritius must balance partnerships without allowing security cooperation to erode maritime policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates, fisheries, renewable projects and logistics in Western Sahara remain tied to Morocco's sovereignty strategy and face legal and diplomatic contestation. European and African partners increasingly weigh commercial access against recognition risks.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: The Tanger Med and Atlantic port networks deepen Morocco's role as a Europe-Africa gateway, while Gulf, Chinese, European and U.S. capital compete for influence. Dependence on imported energy and technology remains a counterweight to Rabat's growing leverage.

highlights: Cabo Delgado LNG restart remains pivotal
Maputo seeks tighter control over gas revenues

frictionVectors.title: LNG Security and Foreign Operators
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence in Cabo Delgado continues to constrain LNG development and leaves major projects dependent on foreign security support. International operators retain substantial leverage over financing, technology, and project timelines.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mozambique remains reliant on external lenders and contractors for ports, railways, and energy infrastructure, limiting near-term state control over strategic corridors and future revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of New Energy Assets
frictionVectors.details: International oil majors and foreign-backed consortiums are positioned to dominate upstream development, creating pressure for stronger local-content rules and revenue safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Uranium, lithium, and rare-earth projects draw competing Chinese, European, and Gulf interests. Namibia is attempting to retain more downstream value while avoiding overdependence on any single partner.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control and improved terms from foreign mining interests, especially in uranium. Political confrontation with France has increased uncertainty over technical capacity, markets, and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Pipeline and Regional Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Attacks and diplomatic tensions affecting the Benin export corridor threaten Niger's access to oil revenues. Sanctions, border closures, and expanding Russian security ties further complicate infrastructure protection.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Production Losses
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, sabotage, and insecurity in the Niger Delta continue to reduce public revenues and weaken federal control over critical infrastructure. International oil companies remain influential in production and technical operations.

frictionVectors.title: Refinery and Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: The Dangote refinery improves Nigeria's bargaining position, but fuel logistics, gas supply, and financing still depend on complex private and foreign-linked networks. Regulatory disputes may determine how much value remains domestically.

highlights: State control remains strong, external pressure rises
Mineral diplomacy collides with DRC conflict

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral and Security Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Accusations that Rwanda supports M23 continue to generate sanctions threats and diplomatic pressure, while regional mineral flows expose Kigali to scrutiny over supply-chain transparency and sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Strategic Dependency
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong administrative control over national infrastructure and resources but remains exposed to Western aid conditionality, security partnerships, and changing donor attitudes over the DRC conflict.

highlights: Maritime security is central to sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE HYDROCARBON UNCERTAINTY
frictionVectors.details: Exploration partnerships have yet to produce commercial output, leaving the country dependent on external capital while retaining limited bargaining leverage over its maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA FISHING PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Illegal, underreported and foreign-linked fishing activity challenges enforcement of São Tomé and Príncipe's large maritime zone and limits local capture of fisheries value.

highlights: New oil and gas era begins

frictionVectors.title: CONTRACT AND LOCAL-CONTENT REVIEW
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater national participation and revised terms in oil, gas and mining, creating friction with incumbent international operators and financiers.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE BORDER AND FISHERIES MANAGEMENT
frictionVectors.details: The Senegal-Mauritania offshore gas relationship is strategically important, while industrial and foreign fishing pressure continues to test coastal resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN FISHING ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles relies on external fleets and investment to monetize tuna resources, creating persistent concerns over licensing transparency, value capture and ecological sustainability.

frictionVectors.title: INDIAN OCEAN STRATEGIC COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Port, maritime-security and connectivity partnerships involving India, France, China and other actors offer benefits but constrain the space for fully independent strategic choices.

highlights: Mining growth outpaces domestic value capture

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore operations and associated logistics remain reliant on foreign capital and export infrastructure, limiting domestic control over pricing, processing and supply-chain value.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAILWAY LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Mining-linked rail and port projects can improve connectivity but risk concentrating strategic infrastructure around exporters rather than broad-based national industrial development.

frictionVectors.title: SOMALILAND AND RED SEA ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Disputes involving Somaliland, Ethiopia and the federal government continue to affect control of ports, maritime boundaries and prospective offshore resources despite diplomatic de-escalation efforts.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL SECURITY AND PORT PARTNERSHIPS
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states and other external actors provide security and infrastructure support, but their competing interests can dilute federal control over ports, logistics corridors and resource concessions.

highlights: Grid and port bottlenecks constrain leverage

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL-MINERALS CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: South Africa retains substantial mineral and processing capacity, but foreign investment and downstream technology remain important in platinum, manganese, battery minerals, and renewables.

frictionVectors.title: LOGISTICS AND POWER
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages, rail failures, and port congestion weaken state control over export corridors and increase reliance on private operators and external capital.

highlights: Oil lifeline exposed to regional war
Weak state control over production corridors

frictionVectors.title: SUDAN OIL TRANSIT
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on pipelines and export infrastructure crossing Sudan, leaving its primary revenue source vulnerable to conflict, political leverage, and transit disruption.

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE-REVENUE CAPTURE
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues remain concentrated among political and security elites, while foreign operators and neighboring states retain significant influence over production, transport, and payments.

highlights: War fragments control of gold and ports
External patrons compete for strategic access

frictionVectors.title: GOLD ECONOMY
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling networks finance rival armed actors and attract competing regional and international intermediaries, sharply reducing civilian state control.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and prospective Red Sea infrastructure have become strategic assets contested through military alliances, foreign security relationships, and commercial access arrangements.

highlights: Resource nationalism paired with selective openness

frictionVectors.title: LNG AND MINING NEGOTIATIONS
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking greater domestic value capture from natural gas and minerals, but major projects still depend on foreign financing, technology, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: PORT-CORRIDOR DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Dar es Salaam and emerging rail and road corridors increase regional leverage, while concessions and external infrastructure finance create continuing sovereignty concerns.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional logistics hinge
Small-state autonomy balanced by external capital

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND TRANSIT INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé gives Togo significant regional leverage, but its expansion and logistics ecosystem remain exposed to foreign operators, lenders, and shifting West African trade politics.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE VALUE CAPTURE
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains strategic phosphate assets, yet limited domestic processing and dependence on external technology and markets constrain sovereign control over the full value chain.

highlights: State Tightens Control Over Strategic Sectors

frictionVectors.title: European Migration and Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains dependent on European cooperation, trade, and financial support, giving outside actors influence over domestic and border policy. Disputes over migration management periodically strain relations.

frictionVectors.title: Gas Import and Electricity Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on imported energy, especially Algerian gas and fuel, constrains Tunisia's strategic autonomy. Aging infrastructure and fiscal pressures limit rapid diversification.

frictionVectors.title: Tilenga-EACOP Financing and Environmental Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's oil corridor is backed by major regional and foreign investment but faces sustained opposition over land acquisition, environmental risk, and financing restrictions. The project deepens state revenue ambitions while increasing external scrutiny.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese lenders and contractors remain important to transport, energy, and industrial projects. Debt-servicing pressure and opaque contracting can narrow Kampala's room for independent infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt attract competing Chinese, Western, Gulf, and regional interests, giving Zambia bargaining power but exposing it to external pressure. The central challenge is converting mineral demand into domestic refining, jobs, and fiscal capture.

frictionVectors.title: Power Shortages Threaten Mining Control
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortfalls and climate-related drought have disrupted electricity supply to mines and industry. Emergency imports and private generation increase costs and weaken the state's ability to set favorable terms for mineral processing.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and Platinum Ownership Contest
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is seeking greater local processing and state participation in lithium, platinum, and other minerals, but remains reliant on foreign capital, technology, and export markets. Regulatory uncertainty and opaque ownership structures complicate sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Currency Fragility
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and recurring currency instability raise operating costs and push producers toward offshore financing and payment arrangements. These pressures reduce Harare's leverage over strategic exporters and infrastructure providers.
